e-9866.knowledge_point: Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of X
e-9866.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x = t-\sin t, \quad y = 1-\cos t, \quad t\in \left[0,\pi\right].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis?
e-9866.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=0$ to $t_2=\pi.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\sin^2 t +\cos^2 t= 1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\sqrt{2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{3}}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=cos⁡2t,y=cos⁡t,t∈[0,π4]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
π∫0π/4cos2⁡tsin⁡t16cos2⁡t−1dt
b
π∫0π/4cos2⁡tsin⁡t9sin2⁡t−1dt
c
2π∫0π/4cos2⁡tsin⁡t8cos2⁡t+1dt
d
2π∫0π/4cos⁡tsin⁡t16cos2⁡t+1dt
e
2π∫0π/4cos⁡tsin2⁡t9cos2⁡t+1dt

decision.explanation: For rotation about the x-axis, S=2π∫y√((x′)²+(y′)²) dt. Here x′=-2sin(2t)=-4sin(t)cos(t) and y′=-sin(t), so the speed is sin(t)√(16cos²(t)+1), since sin(t)≥0 on [0,π/4]. Multiplying by y=cos(t) gives option d.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{4}].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡2t=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t(16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot |\operatorname{sin}⁡t|\cdot \sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=π4.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(cos⁡2t)=−2sin⁡2tdydt=ddt(cos⁡t)=−sin⁡t.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t(−2sin⁡2t)2+(−sin⁡t)2dt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t4sin2⁡2t+sin2⁡tdt.

Now, using the identity sin⁡2t=2sin⁡tcos⁡t, we can rewrite our integral as follows:

S=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t4sin2⁡2t+sin2⁡tdt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t4(2sin⁡tcos⁡t)2+sin2⁡tdt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t16sin2⁡tcos2⁡t+sin2⁡tdt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡tsin2⁡t(16cos2⁡t+1)dt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t⋅sin2⁡t⋅16cos2⁡t+1dt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡t⋅|sin⁡t|⋅16cos2⁡t+1dt=2π∫0π/4cos⁡tsin⁡t16cos2⁡t+1dt

content.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{4}].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡2t=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t(16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot |\operatorname{sin}⁡t|\cdot \sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=cos⁡t,y=et,t∈[0,1]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
2π∫01etsin2⁡t+e2tdt
b
2π∫01e2tsin⁡tdt
c
2π∫01et(sin⁡t+et)dt
d
2π∫01sin⁡tcos2⁡t+e2tdt
e
4π∫01tsin⁡t+etdt
Submit

decision.explanation: Rotation about the x-axis gives S=2π∫y√((x′)²+(y′)²) dt. Here x′=-sin(t), y′=e^t, and y=e^t>0. Thus S=2π∫₀¹e^t√(sin²(t)+e^(2t)) dt, which is option a.
